chunks: Deliberate killing is every [act] in which the striking was intended, so upon him is retaliation (qisas); and rather, the erroneous [killing] is that he intends the thing but hits another.
And he said: When he confesses against himself with the killing, he is killed, even if there is no proof against him.

key_terms.أَقَرَّ: Iqrar — confession, a self-incriminating admission recognized as a binding form of legal proof in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.الْخَطَأُ: Al-khata' — erroneous/accidental killing, where the perpetrator intended to strike a different target
key_terms.الْقَوَدُ: Al-qawad — retaliation (qisas), the right of the victim's family to demand equal retribution through execution of the killer
key_terms.بَيِّنَةٌ: Bayyina — legal proof through witnesses, the standard evidentiary requirement in Islamic courts
key_terms.قَتْلُ الْعَمْدِ: Deliberate killing — intentional homicide in which the perpetrator both intended the blow and used a lethal means

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on deliberate killing and what happens when a killer confesses without witnesses?
ai.summary: This hadith from the 5th or 6th Imam defines the legal distinction between deliberate murder (al-qatl al-'amd) and erroneous killing (al-khata'), establishing that deliberate murder mandates retaliation (al-qawad/qisas). The second ruling establishes that a voluntary confession to murder is sufficient for capital punishment, even without independent corroborating witnesses. In classical Shia jurisprudence, this highlights the binding power of iqrar (confession) as a form of legal proof in qisas cases, where the defendant's own admission supersedes the need for external witnesses (bayyina). This ruling was especially significant for early Muslim jurists adjudicating cases where witnesses were unavailable.
